name: Nose-lifting or slimming massage

lead: Nose massage is the practice of pressing, pinching or rubbing the nose, often daily, in the hope of making it narrower, higher-bridged or more lifted. It is described in beauty and appearance communities as a no-cost, non-surgical option.

Proponents say repeated pressure gradually reshapes the nose. Surgeons quoted about similar pressure methods say bone and cartilage are not changed by outside pressure, and no published studies testing the practice were located.

paras: Users press along the sides and bridge of the nose or pinch the tip for a few minutes, usually daily as part of a skincare or face routine. It needs no equipment.
No documented harms specific to the practice were located. General skin irritation from frequent rubbing is possible.

angle.text: Beauty communities describe daily nose rubbing or pinching as a free, non-surgical way to slim or lift the nose through gradual tissue reshaping. The claim rests on anecdote, and no studies have tested it.

lead: Nose-lifting or slimming massage is a self-care routine in which people press, pinch, stroke or rub the nose, often daily, hoping to make it look narrower, higher at the bridge or more lifted. It is described in beauty and appearance communities as a no-cost, non-surgical way to refine the centre of the face, and it is usually practised as a few minutes of massage added to a skincare or facial-massage routine.

The idea is that repeated gentle pressure along the bridge and sides of the nose gradually changes its outline. This is a claim made by practitioners; no published study has tested it. For context, the external nose gets its shape mainly from the nasal bones, the nasal cartilages and the bridge, with skin and soft tissue over them [1], and permanent reshaping is the domain of rhinoplasty, where surgeons separate skin from the framework and reshape the structures beneath [2].
Surgeons quoted in coverage of related pressure methods such as nose taping say non-surgical pressure cannot alter bone or cartilage [3].

paras: Proponents describe repeated manual pressure or stroking along the bridge and sides of the nose, sometimes combined with facial massage routines. The practice is related to nose taping and other pressure-based approaches that aim to change nasal shape without surgery [3].

The upper nose is framed by the nasal bones and the lower nose is supported by septal, lateral and alar cartilages, with the alar cartilages defining the tip; skin is thickest at the tip and thinner over the bridge [1]. Shape depends mainly on these bone and cartilage structures [1]. Surgeons' position, as reported in coverage of nose taping, is that permanent reshaping requires surgery and that outside pressure cannot alter bone or cartilage [3].

Rhinoplasty reshapes the nose for appearance or breathing, using open or closed approaches, with swelling that can take a year or more to settle [2]. Massage routines are discussed as a hands-only alternative with no downtime.
